One common example of stock price manipulation is known as "wash trading," where a significant number of shares are traded or converted from one security to another, rather than from the actual share ownership to the market, to create the appearance of a larger volume of activity.

To manipulate stock prices, individuals may use a variety of tactics, such as creating artificial demand by sending false or exaggerated purchase orders, during times when the markets are low or uncertain, to encourage buying. Alternatively, manipulating stock prices can also occur during periods of peak demand when investors are looking to purchase shares at a higher price. By implementing techniques such as creating a "buying frenzy" during times of high demand or forming a specific group of investors as a "hedgitford," these individuals can drive share prices up as long as the demand for their preferred stock remains.

Another practice used by stock manipulators is "wash selling," where large quantities of shares are sold or converted to another stock in the same sector or security during periods of high demand. This can be done in an effort to keep the bought shares consistently in the market while limiting the potential loss on them. This action can also create false signals about the demand and value of a particular stock, giving the manipulator, or their opponents, an unfair advantage.
